analysis.one_liner: Gave tax-free gains to buyers of troubled mortgages and required the wind-down of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, markup, or vote in either chamber during the 110th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Introduced a month into the 2008 financial panic, the bill would have rewritten tax law in three ways favoring investors and corporations: buyers of distressed mortgages and mortgage securities sold before 2010 would have paid zero capital gains tax for the first two years, corporations could have carried recent losses back five years for immediate tax refunds, and multinationals could have brought foreign profits home while deducting 85% of them. It would have repealed the Community Reinvestment Act, which requires banks to serve the communities where they take deposits, and created an FDIC program to shore up troubled banks. It also would have forced Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac out of government conservatorship within two years and then wound them down and dissolved them over a decade, while capping their mortgage portfolios, restoring lower loan limits, and charging them for the federal guarantee behind their debt.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors and funds buying distressed mortgages and mortgage-backed securities would owe no capital gains tax on early sales. Corporations with recent losses would collect refunds years sooner. Multinationals would pay tax on only 15% of repatriated foreign profits. Banks holding Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac preferred stock could deduct their losses as ordinary losses. Troubled banks could receive FDIC-issued capital certificates. Critics of Fannie and Freddie would get their long-sought dismantling of the two housing giants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Distressed-asset buyers, multinationals, banks, and Fannie/Freddie critics

how_it_helps.text: Buyers of residential or commercial mortgages and related securities issued on or before March 14, 2008, and acquired before 2010, would exclude 100% of their gains from income for two years after enactment, then 67% and 33% before the exclusion phases out.
Corporations with net operating losses in 2007 through 2009 could carry those losses back five years, converting paper losses into immediate cash refunds.

Multinationals electing the provision could deduct 85% of cash dividends from foreign subsidiaries, provided the company adopts a board-approved plan to reinvest the money in the United States; the allowed uses include job retention, infrastructure, research, or the 'financial stabilization of the corporation.'

Banks and thrift holding companies holding Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac preferred stock, or that sold it in 2008, would treat the gain or loss as ordinary income or loss, a more valuable deduction than capital-loss treatment.

The FDIC would buy capital in troubled insured banks through a net worth certificate program modeled on the 1982 savings-and-loan program, with limits on executive pay and no direct Treasury appropriation.

The FHFA director would have to terminate the Fannie/Freddie conservatorship within 24 to 30 months if the companies are deemed viable, or put them into receivership if not; surviving firms would face an $850 billion cap on mortgage portfolios, mandatory charter renewals, a 10-year wind-down, payment of state and local taxes, and charges covering the full value of the federal guarantee on their debt.

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury would collect less revenue from the capital gains exclusion, loss carrybacks, and repatriation deduction. Banks would no longer have a Community Reinvestment Act obligation to lend in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. Mortgage borrowers in high-cost areas would face tighter credit as conforming loan limits are rolled back and Fannie and Freddie are barred from buying mortgages above the local median home price, and the eventual dissolution of the two companies would remove a major source of mortgage liquidity.
analysis.who_pays_short: Treasury, underserved borrowers, and mortgage credit markets

drawbacks.text: The tax provisions would sharply reduce federal revenue: 100% capital gains exclusion on troubled-asset sales, five-year loss carrybacks, and an 85% deduction on repatriated foreign profits.
The bill repeals the Community Reinvestment Act of 1977 outright, ending the requirement that banks help meet the credit needs of the low- and moderate-income communities where they operate.

Requiring Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to exit conservatorship within two years and then wind down over a decade, with portfolio caps and a ban on purchasing mortgages above local median home prices, could tighten mortgage credit and raise borrowing costs, particularly in high-cost housing markets.

The repatriation benefit hinges on a reinvestment plan written and approved by the company's own executives and board, with allowed uses as broad as 'financial stabilization of the corporation,' leaving companies rather than the government to decide how the money is actually used.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill responded to a real emergency, and the FDIC capital program and a full charge for the Fannie/Freddie federal guarantee were defensible crisis measures. But most of the bill's value flowed through the tax code to investors in distressed assets, corporations with losses, and multinationals holding foreign profits, with no guaranteed job creation in return, and repealing the Community Reinvestment Act would have stripped protections from underserved borrowers. The Fannie/Freddie wind-down was a genuine policy debate about taxpayer exposure versus mortgage availability, debated here with little elaboration.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Financial Services committees the day it was introduced, and no committee acted on it before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King of Iowa introduced the bill on October 3, 2008, joined by nine House Republican cosponsors including Reps. Michele Bachmann, John Linder, and Louie Gohmert.
The same day, it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the Financial Services Committee.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed, and the bill expired with the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, distressed-asset investors, loss-carrying corporations, and multinationals received no new tax breaks, Treasury kept that revenue, and underserved communities kept Community Reinvestment Act protections. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac remained in conservatorship under the government control put in place in September 2008, rather than facing the mandated two-year exit and ten-year dissolution.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers kept lending rules; investors got no tax breaks

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Republican; no Democrat signed on, and no vote was ever taken, so opposition never took the form of a roll call.

industries.industry: Investors and funds buying distressed mortgages and mortgage-backed securities
industries.note: The bill's 100% capital gains exclusion for troubled-asset sales would have let buyers of pre-2008 mortgage paper sell gains tax-free, with the cost falling on federal revenue rather than the buyer.

An 85% deduction on repatriated foreign earnings would have let multinationals bring profits home at a 5.25% effective rate if they filed a self-approved reinvestment plan, transferring revenue from the Treasury to the companies.

industries.industry: Banks holding Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac preferred stock
industries.note: Ordinary-loss treatment would have let banks write off their collapsed GSE preferred holdings more favorably, converting private balance-sheet damage into reduced tax payments.

industries.industry: Corporations with recent net operating losses
industries.note: Five-year carrybacks for 2007-2009 losses would have delivered immediate cash refunds, a benefit concentrated in large firms with big losses.
The FDIC net worth certificate program would have injected capital into banks facing solvency problems while capping their executives' pay, keeping credit flowing without direct taxpayer funds.

The bill would have ended their conservatorship within two to thirty months and dissolved them over ten years, eliminating the government-backed channel through which much of American mortgage lending flows. Supporters saw taxpayer savings; borrowers faced uncertainty about mortgage availability and pricing.
Dissolving Fannie and Freddie and repealing CRA would have opened room for private-label lending, the sector whose mortgage securities were at the center of the 2008 collapse.
